edges.description: WRN is the RecQ helicase that resolves G-quadruplex and four-way-junction structures at telomeric repeats, so its loss acts directly on telomere replication.
Chronic low-grade destabilization of replication forks drives accumulation of chromosomal aberrations.

edges.description: Critically short, unprotected telomeres trigger a persistent DNA damage response and senescence.
Uncapped telomeres promote chromosomal end fusions and telomere sister chromatid exchange.
Accumulated chromosomal aberrations drive clonal evolution toward the characteristic WS neoplasm spectrum.
Loss of proliferative reserve in renewable tissues manifests as the accelerated-aging phenotypes of WS.
The progeroid tissue environment coexists with, rather than causes, the neoplasia risk; both derive from the shared upstream instability.
Late-generation double-null mice demonstrate that telomere exhaustion is what precipitates the WS phenotype from WRN loss.
edges.limitations: The requirement for an engineered telomerase-null background is itself a species difference: laboratory mice have telomeres far longer than humans, so the model reconstructs a human baseline rather than reproducing one. Conclusions about the ordering of events transfer better than conclusions about rates.

edges.description: The double-null mice develop premature death, hair graying, alopecia, osteoporosis, type II diabetes and cataracts.
edges.limitations: Recapitulation is of the progeroid features as a set; the model has not been shown to reproduce the specifically WS-discordant distribution (distal-predominant osteoporosis, posterior subcapsular rather than nuclear cataract) that distinguishes WS from ordinary aging in humans.

edges.description: Wrn deficiency alone does not produce a Werner-like syndrome in mice with long telomeres.
edges.limitations: The failure is attributable to the mouse's long telomere reserve rather than to WRN having a different function in mice, so this model should not be cited as evidence against a WRN-centred mechanism in humans — only against a telomere-independent one.
edges.source: Wrn-null mouse on a telomerase-proficient background

nodes.description: WS fibroblasts have a markedly restricted replicative lifespan and reduced plating efficiency relative to normal fibroblasts cultured in parallel, and accumulate DNA damage foci. Premature exhaustion of the proliferative reserve of mesenchymal and other renewable cell populations is the cellular event most directly connected to the progeroid tissue phenotypes. Crucially, this arm is telomere-dependent rather than a direct consequence of WRN loss: enforced telomerase expression rescues it.

nodes.description: WS confers a strong, type-specific predisposition to a narrow set of neoplasms rather than a general increase in cancer. Six tumor types — thyroid neoplasms, malignant melanoma, meningioma, soft tissue sarcoma, leukemia and pre-leukemic marrow conditions, and primary bone neoplasms — account for about two-thirds of all reported neoplasms in WS patients, and the standardized incidence ratios in Japan-resident patients are elevated for all of these except leukemia. The mesenchymal and neural-crest weighting is the mechanistically informative part: it is the opposite of the epithelial-dominated spectrum of ordinary aging, and is thought to reflect both differential dependence on WRN across lineages and the propensity of sarcomas to maintain telomeres by the recombination-based ALT pathway that WRN normally suppresses.

nodes.description: WS cells display "variegated translocation mosaicism" — multiple, variable, predominantly stable chromosomal rearrangements differing between clones — together with elevated telomere sister chromatid exchange and increased common fragile site expression. This is the mutator phenotype that underlies the WS cancer predisposition, and it is the shared feature that groups WS with the other RecQ disorders (Bloom syndrome, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome) as chromosomal instability syndromes.

nodes.description: Without WRN, cells lose a factor that acts on complex DNA intermediates — G-quadruplexes, Holliday junctions and bubble structures — during replication and repair. WS fibroblasts show a specifically slowed DNA chain elongation rate while their capacity to repair X-ray-induced single-strand breaks and UV damage remains normal, so the primary lesion is in replication handling rather than in excision repair per se. WRN also contributes to double-strand break repair through both non-homologous end joining and end resection during homologous recombination.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical and cell biological studies during the past decade have demonstrated involvements of the WRN protein in multiple DNA transactions, including DNA repair, recombination, replication and transcription.

nodes.description: The organismal phenotype is segmental rather than global: some age-related changes are strikingly accelerated (cataract, hair graying and loss, skin atrophy, osteoporosis, atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes) while others characteristic of normal aging are absent — Alzheimer-type dementia and increased amyloid deposition are not features, and the osteoporosis is worse in distal limb bones than in the vertebral column, the reverse of ordinary aging. The segmental pattern is a substantive constraint on the "accelerated aging" framing and should not be smoothed over: WS is not normal aging run fast.

nodes.description: Telomeric TTAGGG repeats form G-quadruplex structures that are preferred WRN substrates, and telomere replication requires resolution of four-way junctions at D- and T-loops. In the absence of WRN these structures persist, the G-rich strand is replicated late or incompletely, and telomere repeats are lost from individual sister chromatids. This node is what converts a cell-autonomous replication defect into a clock: the mouse genetics show that WRN loss alone is nearly silent while telomeres remain long, and that the WS phenotype appears only once telomere reserves are exhausted.

nodes.description: Wrn-null mice on a telomerase-proficient background are essentially unaffected, which for years made WS look untranslatable to the mouse. Crossing Wrn deficiency onto a Terc-null background and breeding to late generations exhausts the mouse's long telomere reserve and unmasks a Werner-like syndrome. The model is therefore not merely a WS mouse but the experiment that identified telomere attrition as the missing variable.

nodes.description: Biallelic null variants in WRN abolish a 1,432-amino-acid nuclear protein that combines an ATP-dependent 3'->5' DNA helicase with an N-terminal 3'->5' exonuclease domain. The combination of the two catalytic activities in one polypeptide is unique among the five human RecQ helicases. Most disease alleles are stop codons, small indels or splice variants that truncate the protein and remove its C-terminal nuclear localization signal, so the residual product is excluded from the nucleus or degraded; the effect is loss of WRN function rather than a variant protein with altered activity.
